Paint it Back is a thoughtfully designed logic puzzle game that takes the classic nonogram formula and refines it into a polished, content-rich experience that is both relaxing and mentally engaging. Developed and published by Casual Labs, the game places players in the role of a restorer tasked with bringing back a gallery of pixel-art paintings that have been mysteriously erased. Rather than relying on story or spectacle, Paint it Back builds its appeal through clear rules, satisfying progression, and a steady sense of accomplishment that comes from solving increasingly complex puzzles through pure deduction.

At its core, Paint it Back revolves around nonograms, also known as picross or griddlers. Each puzzle presents a grid with numerical clues along the rows and columns, indicating how many consecutive squares should be filled in. Using these clues, players must logically determine which cells to paint and which to leave blank, gradually revealing a complete pixel-art image. The rules are simple, but the execution rewards patience and careful reasoning, as guessing is discouraged and logical consistency is key to success. The controls are intuitive, allowing players to mark filled cells, flag empty ones, and undo actions freely, which encourages experimentation without penalty.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how well it introduces complexity over time. Early puzzles are small and forgiving, acting as gentle tutorials that teach players how to read clues and apply basic logic. As the game progresses, grids grow significantly larger, eventually reaching sizes that require sustained focus and multi-step reasoning to complete. This gradual escalation ensures that newcomers are never overwhelmed while still offering a meaningful challenge for experienced puzzle fans. Larger puzzles can take considerable time to solve, but they rarely feel unfair, as solutions are always rooted in logic rather than obscure tricks.

The structure of the game reinforces this sense of steady progression. Paint it Back features a large collection of puzzles spread across multiple themed rooms, each with its own visual identity and tone. Completing puzzles restores paintings to the gallery, providing a clear visual reward that makes progress feel tangible. The pixel-art images themselves are charming and varied, ranging from playful and humorous scenes to more intricate and detailed compositions. This visual payoff adds motivation, as each solved puzzle feels like uncovering a small piece of art rather than simply clearing a grid.

Beyond the main puzzle sets, the game offers additional modes and challenges that significantly enhance replay value. Optional challenge modes introduce constraints such as time pressure or reduced marking tools, appealing to players who want to test their mastery of the mechanics. Randomized or special-condition puzzles ensure that even after completing the main gallery, there is still plenty to engage with. For players who enjoy completionist goals, achievements and optional challenges provide long-term objectives without detracting from the relaxed core experience.

Presentation is clean and functional, prioritizing clarity above all else. The interface stays out of the way, allowing the grid and clues to remain the central focus at all times. Animations and effects are subtle, reinforcing the calm, methodical pace of the game. Sound design follows the same philosophy, with gentle background music and unobtrusive effects that support concentration rather than distract from it. This makes Paint it Back especially well suited for long play sessions or for unwinding after more intense games.

While the game excels at what it sets out to do, its appeal is naturally limited to fans of logic-based puzzles. Players looking for narrative depth, fast-paced gameplay, or mechanical variety beyond nonograms may find the experience too focused or repetitive. However, this narrow focus is also what allows the game to feel so refined, as every system serves the central puzzle-solving experience without unnecessary embellishment.

Overall, Paint it Back stands as an excellent example of a classic puzzle concept executed with care and confidence. It offers a substantial amount of content, a well-balanced difficulty curve, and a soothing presentation that makes logic puzzles feel rewarding rather than stressful. For fans of nonograms or anyone looking for a thoughtful, low-pressure game that rewards patience and reasoning, it delivers a deeply satisfying experience that can be enjoyed in short sessions or long, immersive stretches alike.

Paint it Back is a cool nonogram puzzle game, where you need to use logic to fill the correct squares in a grid, representing an image.
Compared to similar titles on Steam, this one seems to lack some quality-of-life features. However, you also have to consider that this is one of the older ones—it's also a mobile port. But it’s still a solid game that I enjoyed, with a nice presentation. There’s no timer, which can be seen as a negative, but I appreciate it because it removes pressure when solving. There are lots of puzzles to solve, plus Steam Workshop support. The soundtrack is very limited, so listen to your own music instead.
Bigger puzzles have a difficulty selection, which breaks them down into smaller sections. I still recommend going for the full picture since that’s the original puzzle. They can get big, with a size over 30x30, and some can take over an hour. Also, I can confirm that every puzzle can be beaten using logic without guessing. However, the difficulty is all over the place—the hardest puzzles to solve are usually in the middle of a chapter, followed by easier ones. There are in-game achievements, and the credits roll when you get them all.
So, overall, I can recommend this game if you’re a fan of nonograms or puzzle games in general. Despite some shortcomings, it has a ton of content and it’s enjoyable.

[i]Paint it Back[/i] is a wonderful addition to the Steam Picross/Nonogram puzzle library, and is a fantastic starting point for people who are not die-hard fans of the genre. I've included a list of the usual features this game has and doesn't have for people who are familiar with the gametype and want to know in the bottom of my review.

The main thing that sets [i]Paint it Back[/i] apart from its peers is its accessibility features, hence why I say it is a good starting point. Its "Helping Hand" feature highlights rows/column numbers in which progress could be made in the puzzle, providing some 'training wheels' to those who are more inexperienced with the puzzle type. This is a feature that is not often seen in these types of games. Additionally, while the game has larger puzzles (the largest of which being 36x40), you have the option of playing these puzzles on a "lower difficulty", in which the game will section off the larger puzzles into smaller sections. For example, a 20x20 puzzle may become four separate 10x10 puzzles. While I personally didn't use either of these features in my playthrough my first Picross game had a feature similar to the "Helping Hand", and it helped me to learn the ropes.

The other thing that is particularly notable is the game's polish. The animations, art style, and soundtrack are all well-executed. The tracks did not become grating even after my 20-hour complete playthrough, and the game oozes charm in both its aesthetic and its puzzle names.

There is a mode in which you will be presented with a random level from the base game, with the ability to earn medals for: completing the level within a certain time, completing the level while only erasing less than a certain number of cells, and completing the level while only using the X (or cross-out) feature a certain number of times. The requirements are relatively generous, but for my fellow achievement hunters, prepare for a time sink on levels you have already played.



Completing all of the achievements (which includes completing every individual puzzle and then a few other, more gimmicky solves) took me just over 20 hours. I make no claims to be a Nonogram expert, or a particularly fast puzzler, but I have quite a bit of experience with the puzzle type. There is also quite a range of difficulty: some of the later puzzles are quite challenging. In my opinion, there is quite a lot of content being offered for the price, especially if you pick it up during a sale.



I have included a list of features that the game has:

[h2] Nonogram Features [/h2]

[ ✓ ] Auto-Gray Out Solved Numbers
[ ✓ ] Ability to Color/Cross-out/Uncolor Multiple Cells at Once
[ ✓ ] Puzzles Able to be Completed Without Guesswork
[ ✓ ] Division of Board into Evenly Spaced Sections
[ ✓ ] Absence of a Lives System
[ ✓ ] (Optional) Highlight Actionable Rows/Columns

[ X ] Display of Counts on Multi-Select
[ X ] Ability to Set Tentative Squares for Induction Purposes

One feature that is unique to this game ties with the absence of having the count be displayed for multi-select. The game does not lock you to a row or column as most others do. Rather, the game allows you to color wherever you want, potentially allowing you to complete a level in "one brush stroke". This is not an oversight, there are two achievements for doing just that. I find this decision bizarre, but it didn't impede my gameplay enough to mar my overall opinion.

Having played quite a lot of Paint it Back and Pepper's Puzzles - probably among the best nonogram games on Steam - I'll simply offer a comparison of the two.

Paint it Back has better art, which is both more creative and better drawn. The difficulty curve is much smoother and more gradual in Paint it Back. But the user interface is a bit clunky, requiring more clicks than necessary, and missing some obvious quality-of-life features, like the ability to put down "marks" with a single action (e.g. middle mouse button, shift-click, or something), the ability to have more than one puzzle in progress at a time, etc. Paint it Back's puzzles are untimed, so there is no pressure. Paint it Back also offers a demo, so you can try before you buy.

Pepper's Puzzles is pretty much the reverse of what I wrote above. The art is a bit worse, and less creative, and the difficulty ramps up very steeply. On the other hand, it has a better, smoother user interface, better music, and an overall better experience. Pepper's Puzzles has a timer, and gives you a number of stars based on how quickly you solved each puzzle. The timer is generous, but still adds pressure to solve the puzzle quickly. This may be a positive or negative. I enjoy the pressure and challenge, but if I fail to get three stars, I don't enjoy being "forced" to re-solve the puzzle. To be clear, there's nothing in the game forcing you to re-solve anything and stars are basically meaningless; you could ignore the timer entirely if you like. It's just my completionist impulse. Pepper's Puzzles has no demo.

Both games offer a huge number of puzzles to solve. Overall, I've been playing more of Paint it Back than Pepper's Puzzles, simply because the art is better which makes the puzzles more fun to solve.

A great picross/nonogram game with plenty of replay value. I found this game very relaxing.

Pros:
- Regular levels are not timed.
- Regular levels do not have any penalty for clicking the wrong square; you are free to click and unclick any square you want.
- Good variety of difficulty levels.
- The larger puzzles give you an option of dividing them up into smaller grids to work on, which can be much easier than tackling the entire puzzle grid at once.
- 33hrs of playtime (til all achievements unlocked) and I'm not even bored of the game yet.

Cons:
- The game marks the grid into sections of either 4 or 5 - not 5x5 which is usual for these puzzles. Additionally some puzzles have rows in multiple of 4 while having the columns in multiples of 5. 
This means you may have to manually count each square you mark, if you usually rely on 5x5 grid markers to count quickly.
While the game does mark the 4 and 5 in different colours, I found it hard to notice the different colours and as a result often failed to notice that it was 4x4 or 4x5, instead of 5x5.

Other:
- When you click and drag it will paint multiple squares, but this won't be restricted to only squares in the row you begun in. This makes it easy to accidentally click the wrong squares, which isn't too much of a problem unless you are playing the Masterpiece Mystery levels and trying to get the ribbon for not making mistakes.
- At the end you have access to a "Mystery" room where the game will select a random masterpiece for you to work on, without you knowing which painting it is. These paintings are all from the game, there are no randomly generated ones.
